intro.speaker: archive
intro.text: You are sealed inside a vault of old training logs. Something deep in these networks refuses to learn, and the door will not open until you understand why.

intro.speaker: archive
intro.text: Three rooms wait. Each one holds a piece of the puzzle.

rooms.title: The error chamber
rooms.description: Two chalkboards face each other, one marked 20-LAYER, one marked 56-LAYER, both covered in rising error curves.

rooms.title: The suspects room
rooms.description: A corkboard pins up two crossed-out culprits — OVERFITTING and VANISHING GRADIENTS — next to a stack of batch-normalization printouts.

rooms.title: The filing room
rooms.description: Three drawers sit under a diagram of a looping wire, labelled RESIDUAL FUNCTION, IDENTITY MAPPING, and SHORTCUT CONNECTION.

rooms.title: The solver's desk
rooms.description: A half-finished equation sits on the desk, F(x) waiting to be pushed toward zero.

boss.mechanicReason: Frame boss: rebuild the chain of reasoning from broken depth to the residual fix.

item.prompt: The vault door wants the story of the degradation problem told in the right order.

steps.text: A deeper plain network is trained and shows higher training error than its shallower counterpart.
Overfitting and vanishing gradients are both ruled out as the cause.
The layers are reformulated to fit a residual function F(x) = H(x) - x, added back to x via an identity shortcut.

item.why: This is the order in which the passage builds its case: observe the problem, rule out the obvious causes, then introduce the fix.

sourceRefs.quote: the solvers may simply drive the weights of the multiple nonlinear lay- ers toward zero to approach identity mappings.

hints: Start with what Figure 1 showed, then think about what got ruled out before the fix was introduced.

outro.speaker: archive
outro.text: The chalkboards go dark and the drawers slide shut. You've traced the fault line from broken depth to the residual fix — the door opens.

intro.speaker: archive
intro.text: Deeper in the vault lie the blueprints for building these networks at scale, and a courtroom of claims about whether depth always wins.

rooms.title: The shortcut office
rooms.description: Three labeled folders sit on a desk: OPTION A, OPTION B, OPTION C, each with a different rule for handling dimension mismatches.

rooms.title: The bottleneck workshop
rooms.description: A conveyor belt narrows in the middle, flanked by crates labeled 1x1, 3x3, and 1x1 again.

rooms.title: The verdict hall
rooms.description: A judge's bench is piled with test-error reports, including one marked 1202-LAYERS stamped WORSE THAN EXPECTED.

rooms.title: The detector's booth
rooms.description: Two camera rigs sit side by side, one labeled VGG-16 and one labeled RESNET-101, aimed at the same test image.

boss.mechanicReason: Frame boss: apply the level's reasoning about depth and shortcut design to a single conclusive judgment.

item.scenario: A colleague argues: 'Since the 1202-layer network trained to under 0.1% training error with no optimization difficulty, and residual networks keep gaining accuracy from depth, this 1202-layer model must also have the best test accuracy of all the CIFAR-10 models tested.'

options.text: No — the 1202-layer network actually tested worse than the 110-layer network, likely due to overfitting on the small dataset.
options.feedback: Correct. Training without optimization difficulty is not the same as best test accuracy; the passage attributes the 1202-layer network's worse test result to overfitting.

options.text: Yes — more depth with no optimization difficulty always produces the best test accuracy in this paper's experiments.
options.feedback: The passage directly reports the opposite for the 1202-layer network: despite training almost perfectly, its test result was worse than the 110-layer network's.

options.text: Yes — because the three shortcut options A, B, and C all showed the 1202-layer setup being best for test accuracy.
options.feedback: Options A/B/C are about shortcut handling for dimension changes, not about the 1202-layer depth experiment, and they don't support this claim.

sourceRefs.quote: The testing result of this 1202-layer network is worse than that of our 110-layer network
Our method shows no optimization difficulty, and this 103-layer network is able to achieve training error <0.1%

hints: Training without optimization difficulty is not the same thing as generalizing well on the test set.

outro.speaker: archive
outro.text: The verdict is read, the camera rigs power down, and the vault's final door swings wide. You judged depth correctly, where it helps and where it doesn't.
